cards.q: What is an Ethernet frame?
cards.a: An Ethernet frame is the Layer 2 data unit used to transport upper-layer protocols such as IPv4, IPv6, and ARP across an Ethernet network. A switch examines the destination MAC, source MAC, VLAN information, and other Layer 2 fields to make forwarding decisions.

cards.q: What is the overall structure of a standard Ethernet frame?
cards.a: Preamble (7 B) | SFD (1 B) | Dest MAC (6 B) | Src MAC (6 B) | optional 802.1Q tag (4 B) | Type/Length (2 B) | Payload (46-1500 B) | FCS (4 B).

cards.q: What are the Preamble and SFD in an Ethernet frame?
cards.a: The Preamble is 7 bytes and provides synchronization. The SFD (Start Frame Delimiter) is 1 byte and indicates the frame is about to begin. Together they are 8 bytes transmitted on the wire but are not normally included in the Ethernet frame size.

cards.q: What forwarding behavior does an Ethernet switch apply based on the destination MAC?
cards.a: Known unicast is forwarded toward the learned port, unknown unicast is flooded within the VLAN, broadcast is flooded within the VLAN, and multicast forwarding depends on multicast/switch configuration.

cards.q: What is the switch exam rule for Destination MAC and Source MAC?
cards.a: Destination MAC is used for the forwarding decision, while Source MAC is used for MAC address learning. Source MAC -> learn, Destination MAC -> forward.

cards.q: What does the 2-byte Type/Length field represent?
cards.a: It can represent a Length in IEEE 802.3 framing or an EtherType in Ethernet II framing. Values greater than or equal to 0x0600 are interpreted as EtherTypes.

cards.q: Which EtherTypes map to which protocols?
cards.a: 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x0806 = ARP, 0x86DD = IPv6, 0x8100 = IEEE 802.1Q, 0x88A8 = IEEE 802.1ad S-Tag / QinQ.

cards.q: How do you distinguish an EtherType from a 802.3 Length value?
cards.a: Values up to 1500 decimal mean Length; values from 1536 decimal (0x0600) mean EtherType; values 1501 through 1535 are reserved for this distinction.

cards.q: How does Ethernet II framing differ from IEEE 802.3 framing?
cards.a: Ethernet II uses the 2-byte field as an EtherType and is the dominant framing for modern IP networks. IEEE 802.3 can use it as a Length field followed by LLC and sometimes SNAP to identify the upper-layer protocol.

cards.q: What is the structure of an 802.1Q VLAN tag?
cards.a: The 802.1Q tag adds 4 bytes: TPID (2 bytes, standard 0x8100) and TCI (2 bytes) which contains PCP (3 bits, Layer 2 priority/802.1p), DEI (1 bit, Drop Eligibility Indicator), and VLAN ID (12 bits).

cards.q: What is the range of usable VLAN IDs?
cards.a: The VLAN ID field is 12 bits, giving 0-4095, but 0 is reserved for priority tagging and 4095 is reserved, so usable VLAN IDs are commonly 1-4094.

cards.q: How does QinQ (IEEE 802.1ad) tagging work?
cards.a: QinQ stacks multiple VLAN tags: an outer/provider tag with a common TPID of 0x88A8 plus an inner customer tag using 0x8100. This lets service providers transport customer VLANs while adding their own VLAN tag.

cards.q: What is the Ethernet payload size range and when is padding used?
cards.a: The standard Ethernet payload range is 46-1500 bytes. If actual data is smaller than 46 bytes, padding is added to satisfy the minimum Ethernet frame size.

cards.q: What is the FCS and what does it do?
cards.a: The FCS (Frame Check Sequence) is a 4-byte trailer at the end of the frame that uses a CRC-based mechanism to detect transmission errors; a frame that fails the check is discarded. It provides error detection, not correction, and does not cover Preamble/SFD.

cards.q: What is the minimum standard Ethernet frame size and what does it include?
cards.a: 64 bytes, counted from the Destination MAC through the FCS: Dest MAC 6 + Src MAC 6 + Type/Length 2 + Payload/Pad 46 + FCS 4 = 64 bytes. Preamble and SFD are not included.

cards.q: What are the maximum standard Ethernet frame sizes?
cards.a: 1518 bytes for an untagged frame (6+6+2+1500+4) and 1522 bytes for an 802.1Q-tagged frame (the extra 4-byte tag).

cards.q: What is the difference between MTU and Ethernet frame size?
cards.a: MTU is the maximum Layer 3 packet size carried without fragmentation (typically 1500 bytes IP MTU on Ethernet). Frame size is the Layer 2 header + payload + Layer 2 trailer: 14 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes, or 1522 with an 802.1Q tag.

cards.q: What is a runt and what causes it?
cards.a: A runt is an Ethernet frame smaller than the minimum required size, typically under 64 bytes from Destination MAC through FCS. Causes include physical-layer problems, collisions on legacy shared Ethernet, duplex mismatch, and faulty hardware.

cards.q: What are giants and baby giants?
cards.a: A giant exceeds the maximum frame size supported by the interface or platform. A baby giant is slightly larger than the traditional 1518-byte maximum but still accepted by some devices, with 802.1Q-tagged frames (1522 B) as a classic example.

cards.q: Is every frame larger than 1518 bytes an error?
cards.a: No. Legitimate encapsulation can increase Layer 2 size, so frames like 1522-byte 802.1Q-tagged frames are valid. Do not automatically assume oversized frames are errors.

cards.q: What is a jumbo frame?
cards.a: A jumbo frame is an Ethernet frame larger than the standard Ethernet maximum (commonly configured near an MTU of 9000 bytes), but its exact size is implementation-dependent and all devices along the path must support the frame size.

cards.q: What are the core switching model roles for Source MAC, Destination MAC, VLAN Tag, EtherType, and FCS?
cards.a: Source MAC -> Learn, Destination MAC -> Forward, VLAN Tag -> VLAN context, EtherType -> Protocol identification, FCS -> Error detection.

cards.q: Do switches rewrite MAC addresses when forwarding frames?
cards.a: No. Switches normally forward the existing Ethernet frame without rewriting source and destination MAC addresses, which remain the same across the Layer 2 switching path. A router, in contrast, creates a new Layer 2 frame per outgoing segment.

cards.q: Which commands verify interface errors, MAC table, ARP, trunks, and MTU?
cards.a: show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 (look for input errors, CRC, frame, overrun, ignored, output errors), show mac address-table, show arp, show interfaces trunk, and show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 | include MTU.

cards.q: Which field values must be memorized for the Ethernet frame quick review?
cards.a: Preamble 7 B, SFD 1 B, Dest MAC 6 B, Src MAC 6 B, 802.1Q tag 4 B, Type/Length 2 B, Payload 46-1500 B, FCS 4 B, minimum frame 64 B, maximum untagged 1518 B, maximum tagged 1522 B, standard IP MTU 1500 B.

cards.q: What is the one-minute mental model of the Ethernet frame?
cards.a: The frame is a Layer 2 container: Destination MAC drives forwarding, Source MAC drives learning, Type/Length identifies the protocol (EtherType), and FCS provides error detection. Sizes: preamble 7 B, SFD 1 B, tag 4 B optional, payload 46-1500 B, FCS 4 B; min 64 B, max untagged 1518 B, max tagged 1522 B, IP MTU 1500 B.
